# The Hydraulic Siphon: Why Your 2004 Silverado Brakes Fade When the Engine Runs

A brake pedal that feels firm at rest but drops to the floor immediately after starting the engine points directly to a specific hydraulic failure mode. In your 2004 Chevy Silverado 1500, the symptoms you describedâreplacing pads, rotors, calipers, and the master cylinder yet still losing pressureâindicate that air has entered the system or the new components are not sealing against the existing vacuum differential created by the engine.

When you turn off the engine, the brake lines are at atmospheric pressure relative to the reservoir. If there is a minor leak or a compromised seal in the new master cylinder, the fluid just sits there. However, once you start the truck, the power steering pump and alternator begin to create suction on accessories driven by the serpentine belt, but more importantly, the engine creates a slight vacuum in certain intake manifolds. While modern vehicles often have dedicated vacuum pumps for brakes, older GM trucks like the Silverado rely on engine manifold vacuum for specific actuators.

The critical issue here is likely the interaction between the master cylinder reservoir and the hydraulic circuit. If air has entered the system during the replacement of the rear calipers or lines, it will sit in high points until a pressure change forces it into motion. Air is compressible; fluid is not. When you push the pedal with the engine off, you might be compressing a small pocket of air trapped near a bleed nipple or in the reservoir itself, masking the problem. The moment the engine starts, the dynamic changes in pressure can pull that trapped air further into the lines, making the pedal feel like it has lost all resistance instantly.

The standard diagnosis for this symptom is an incomplete bleed or a compromised master cylinder seal that only fails under load. Since you have already replaced the master cylinder, the likelihood of a bad unit is lower unless it was installed with debris in the bore. The most probable cause is air trapped in the rear circuit or the proportioning valve.

To resolve this, you must perform a systematic bleed that accounts for the truck's hydraulic architecture. Start with the wheel furthest from the master cylinder and work your way closer: right rear, left rear, right front, then left front. This sequence prevents you from re-introducing air into already bled lines.

If you are using a manual hand pump or having an assistant press the pedal, ensure the brake fluid reservoir is capped immediately after each cycle to prevent atmospheric pressure from sucking air back in through the open port. Many mechanics leave the cap off during bleeding, which works if done quickly, but it fails if the system contains significant air volume.

Consider installing a vacuum bleeder valve on the master cylinder reservoir. This tool allows you to create negative pressure to pull fluid and air out simultaneously without requiring an assistant. It is significantly faster than the pedal-pump method and reduces the risk of reintroducing air.

If bleeding the rear circuit multiple times yields no results, inspect the proportioning valve located between the front and rear lines. On many Silverados, this component can develop internal leaks or fail to seat properly, causing pressure loss specifically when the engine vacuum interacts with the system dynamics. Replacing the master cylinder is not a guarantee of a fix if the downstream components are also compromised by air ingress.

Finally, verify that the brake fluid is fresh and free of moisture. Old fluid absorbs water from the atmosphere, which lowers the boiling point and can create vapor bubbles under heat. If the fluid is contaminated, it will mimic the behavior of air in the lines, causing a spongy or loose pedal regardless of how well you bleed the system.
